Structure Snowballing (arXiv 2604.06066, April 2026) identifies a related failure mode where constrained decoding pushes models into 'formatting traps' that prevent semantic error correction. Three mitigations exist: CRANE (ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.09061) augments output grammars with reasoning rules, recovering +10pp on symbolic reasoning while maintaining constraints. DCCD (arXiv 2603.03305) uses draft-conditioned constrained decoding—unconstrained draft first, then constrained decoding conditioned on the draft—achieving +24pp on GSM8K.   "approach": "**Architecture overview.** Three architecturally diverse reasoning chains run in parallel on each multimodal math problem, sharing tiered-verified intermediate facts through a central knowledge base (KB). Unlike AG2's SKEST—which benefits from a closed symbolic language and complete deductive engine (DDAR)—general multimodal math involves open-ended natural language assertions requiring a fundamentally different verification architecture. Our key insight is that the SKEST paradigm transfers not as identical formal verification, but as a gracefully-degrading spectrum: formal where possible, visually-grounded where needed, and PRM-scored everywhere.\n\n**Chain specialization with genuine architectural diversity.** Following MEXA's principle that genuine modality specialization requires different model architectures (not merely different prompts or input ablation on the same model family):\n(1) Vision-dominant chain: Kimi K2.6 (1T/32B active MoE, MoonViT-400M vision encoder, 4× H100 FP8). Selected for its state-of-the-art visual perception (87.4% MathVision without tools, 93.2% with Python), native high-resolution image encoding, and 3D ViT temporal compression. Prompted to prioritize diagram interpretation, spatial relationship extraction, and geometric reasoning from visual input.\n(2) Text-dominant chain: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (35B/3B active MoE, 1× H100). A different architecture family (Qwen's MoE with 256 experts, 8 routed + 1 shared per token) receiving text-only problem descriptions plus diagram descriptions extracted by the vision chain. Focuses on algebraic manipulation, equation setup, and symbolic reasoning—leveraging Qwen3.6's strong math performance (92.7 AIME 2026).\n(3) Tool-augmented chain: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (1× H100) generating executable SymPy/Python code in a sandboxed execution environment. Each computation step is executed and its output constitutes a verified fact by construction. This chain can also invoke visual analysis tools à la TIM-PRM's Independent Question Asking.\nThe architectural diversity (Kimi K2.6's MoonViT+MLA attention vs. Qwen3.6's dense-MoE with GQA) ensures genuinely different inductive biases for visual vs. symbolic processing, not merely input filtering.\n\n**'Think-then-Assert' protocol (addressing the Format Tax).** The Format Tax (arXiv 2604.03616) and Structure Snowballing (arXiv 2604.06066) demonstrate 10–30% reasoning degradation from constrained structured output in open-weight models. We adopt a hybrid protocol inspired by DCCD and 'Thinking Before Constraining' (arXiv 2601.07525):\n• Phase 1 (unconstrained reasoning): Each chain generates free-form natural language reasoning for each step with NO formatting constraints. The model reasons naturally, avoiding the cognitive overhead of satisfying format requirements during actual mathematical thought.\n• Phase 2 (constrained assertion extraction): After completing each reasoning step, a designated trigger token (<ASSERT>) activates XGrammar-constrained decoding for ONLY the structured assertion block: {step_id, assertion_type (A–F), formal_repr, dependencies, confidence}. This block is typically 50–100 tokens vs. 200–500 tokens of free-form reasoning, so constraints apply to <25% of total generation.\n• Phase 3 (verification): The extracted assertion enters the tiered verification pipeline.\nThis 'Think-then-Assert' protocol preserves reasoning quality (Phase 1 is fully unconstrained) while ensuring deterministic assertion extraction (Phase 2 is constrained but brief). We empirically measure and report the residual format tax of this hybrid approach vs. fully unconstrained generation as part of our ablation study.\n\nThe assertion_type taxonomy:\n• Type A (Algebraic/Arithmetic): equations, simplifications, identities → formal_repr is SymPy-parseable\n• Type B (Calculus/Analysis): derivatives, integrals, limits → formal_repr is SymPy expression\n• Type C (Coordinate Geometry): distance, angle, area with coordinates → formal_repr is SymPy geometry predicate\n• Type D (Synthetic Geometry): congruence, similarity, circle theorems → formal_repr is predicate-argument structure\n• Type E (Combinatorial/Logical): counting formulas, modular arithmetic → formal_repr is Z3-compatible\n• Type F (Unverifiable): strategy statements, visual descriptions, abstract arguments → no formal_repr\n\n**Three-tier verification pipeline with visual grounding.** Each intermediate assertion passes through:\n• Tier 1 — Formal CAS+SMT verification (Types A, B, C, E): SymPy's equation solver/simplifier/geometry module verifies algebraic/arithmetic/calculus/coordinate facts; Z3 handles inequalities and logical assertions. Following MATH-VF's sparse dependency DAG (each step depends on 2–4 predecessors), verification is O(n·M) where M≤4. For assertions with visual dependencies (e.g., 'the angle shown equals 60°'), we add EVPV-inspired visual premise checking: extract the visual premise ('angle in figure'), verify it against an independently-computed visual constraint (tool-augmented chain re-measures from the image), and gate the formal verification result on visual reliability. Estimated coverage: ~65–75% of Type A/B steps (accounting for visual extraction noise in multimodal settings, down from MATH-VF's 90%+ on text-only), ~60–70% of Type C, ~55–65% of Type E.\n• Tier 2 — Back-translation consistency + visual grounding (Type D): For synthetic geometry claims, we combine HERMES-inspired back-translation with CoRGI-style post-hoc visual grounding. The claim is formalized, checked via coordinate instantiation where possible, and independently grounded in the image by re-querying visual features. Estimated coverage: ~35–45% of Type D steps.\n• Tier 3 — TIM-PRM-enhanced scoring (all types, especially Type F): A process reward model combining FoVer's formally-grounded training methodology with TIM-PRM's Independent Question Asking (IQA) mechanism. For each step, the PRM can independently query the image and external tools to verify premises, decoupling verification from the reasoning chain's own context—addressing TIM-PRM's finding that confirmation bias in same-context verification degrades accuracy. This ensures no intermediate fact is left entirely unscored.\n\n**Cross-chain verified fact sharing via step-boundary injection (KB mechanism specified).** The KB query and injection mechanism operates at reasoning step boundaries with a precisely defined protocol:\n1. Step generation: Chain i generates free-form reasoning for step k (unconstrained, ~2–5 seconds per step at current inference speeds).\n2. Assertion extraction: The <ASSERT> trigger activates constrained decoding for the structured assertion block (~50–100 tokens, <0.5 seconds).\n3. Verification: The assertion enters the tiered pipeline (Tier 1: ~100–200ms for SymPy+Z3; Tier 2: ~500ms for back-translation; Tier 3: ~200ms for PRM scoring). Verification runs asynchronously—the chain can begin its next reasoning step while verification completes.\n4. KB update: Verified assertions are inserted into the KB with status ('formal-verified', 'visual-grounded', 'PRM-scored'), provenance (source chain, step, dependencies), and confidence score.\n5. KB query (every K=3–5 steps): At designated step boundaries, generation PAUSES. The orchestrator queries the KB for assertions relevant to the chain's current reasoning context using embedding similarity (pre-computed assertion embeddings, ~50ms lookup). Relevant cross-chain facts are formatted as a context prefix: 'Verified facts from other chains: [fact1 (formal-verified, confidence 0.95), fact2 (PRM-scored, confidence 0.78)]…'. The chain resumes generation with this augmented context.\n6. KV cache management: Using vLLM's prefix caching, the injected facts extend the KV cache prefix. The overhead per injection is ~50–100ms for context augmentation + KV cache extension, negligible compared to the ~10–25 seconds of total step generation time.\n\nTotal KB query latency per injection: ~100–150ms (50ms embedding lookup + 50–100ms context formatting + cache extension). With K=4 (query every 4 steps) and ~15–25 steps per solution, each chain performs 4–6 KB queries per solution attempt, adding ~0.5–1.0 seconds total overhead per solution—<2% of total generation time.\n\nThe tool-augmented chain's executed code outputs are automatically 'formal-verified' and enter the KB immediately after execution, providing the highest-confidence cross-chain facts.\n\n**Verification coverage analysis with visual dependency accounting (a key contribution).** We provide the first systematic analysis of verification feasibility in multimodal math, explicitly accounting for the visual extraction noise that MATH-VF's text-only analysis does not address:\n• Text-only formalization success (from MATH-VF/SAFE): Algebra 90%+, Coordinate geometry 80%+, Calculus 80%+, Combinatorics 70%+, Synthetic geometry 25–35%\n• Visual extraction accuracy (estimated from MathLens/M3-ACE error analysis): ~80–85% for clear diagrams, ~65–75% for complex/cluttered diagrams\n• Effective multimodal coverage = min(formalization_rate, visual_extraction_accuracy) for visually-dependent assertions:\n  – Algebra+arithmetic (mostly text-dependent): ~80–85% formal coverage, ~55% of MathVista problems\n  – Coordinate geometry (partially visual): ~60–70% effective coverage, ~15% of MathVision\n  – Synthetic geometry (heavily visual): ~15–20% formal + ~35–45% with Tier 2 visual grounding, ~25–35% of MathVision\n  – Calculus (mostly text): ~70–80% formal coverage\n  – Combinatorics (mixed): ~50–60% formal coverage\n  – Overall effective Tier 1+2 coverage: ~45–55% across full benchmarks (lower than R1's inflated 55–65%)\n  – With Tier 3 PRM+IQA: ~85–90% of all steps receive some form of verification scoring\nThis honest, decomposed analysis is itself a contribution: it tells practitioners exactly where formal verification adds value (algebra, arithmetic, coordinate geometry) and where they must rely on softer methods (synthetic geometry, complex visual reasoning).\n\n**Contribution reframing: interpretability and efficiency, not accuracy.** Rather than competing on raw accuracy against Kimi K2.6 (93.2%) or GPT-5.4+Python (96.1%), VeriShare targets three orthogonal contributions:\n(a) **Interpretable verification traces**: Every solution includes a per-step verification report showing formal proof (Tier 1), visual grounding evidence (Tier 2), or PRM reasoning trace with IQA (Tier 3). No existing system—including Kimi K2.6 and GPT-5.4—provides this.\n(b) **Sample efficiency through verified sharing**: We hypothesize that cross-chain verified fact sharing reduces the N in best-of-N sampling needed for a target accuracy. If Chain A formally verifies that x=5 and shares this to Chains B and C, they skip redundant derivation. We measure: accuracy@N curves for VeriShare vs. independent sampling baselines, targeting equivalent accuracy at 2–4× fewer samples.\n(c) **Verification feasibility atlas**: The first domain-decomposed analysis of formal verification coverage on multimodal math, with visual dependency accounting.\n\n**Diverse sampling.** Best-of-N diverse sampling (N=16 per chain, temperature 0.6–0.8), avoiding vLLM's severe beam-search throughput penalties. PRM-BAS demonstrated that PRM-guided selection from diverse samples outperforms naive beam search for multimodal math. VeriShare adds verification-aware selection: solutions with more Tier 1/2 verified steps receive a scoring bonus, biasing toward interpretable solutions.\n\n**Final answer aggregation.** A multimodal PRM (trained following FoVer+TIM-PRM methodology) scores each complete solution path step-by-step, incorporating: (a) per-step PRM quality scores, (b) verification tier bonus (Tier 1 > Tier 2 > Tier 3), (c) cross-chain consistency bonus when verified facts from one chain appear in another's solution, (d) visual grounding reliability score (from EVPV-style checklist matching).\n\n**Ablations (updated).** (1) No sharing: chains run independently, best-of-N selection → isolates sharing contribution to sample efficiency. (2) Unverified sharing: all intermediate facts shared without verification → tests whether verification matters vs. raw fact exchange. (3) Homogeneous chains: all three chains use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with different prompting (no Kimi K2.6) → tests architectural diversity vs. prompting diversity. (4) Single-chain + verification: one chain with Tier 1–3 verification but no parallel sharing → tests single-chain verified reasoning (comparable to ViRC). (5) Format tax measurement: fully unconstrained generation vs. Think-then-Assert vs. full constrained JSON (measuring reasoning degradation from each approach). (6) Verification coverage sweep: vary the verification confidence threshold to trade off coverage vs. precision. (7) Sharing frequency sweep: K=1 (every step) vs. K=3 vs. K=5 vs. K=∞ (no mid-solution sharing, only end-aggregation) → identifies optimal sharing granularity.",

TIM-PRM (Tool-Integrated Multimodal PRM) is a novel agentic framework that transforms verification from a passive classification task into an active, tool-augmented investigation.

## Overview

EVPV (Explicit Visual Premise Verification) is a lightweight verification interface that conditions step scoring on the reliability of the visual premises a step depends on.

## Problem Being Addressed

Vision-language process reward models (VL-PRMs) are increasingly used to score intermediate reasoning steps and rerank candidates under test-time scaling. However, they often function as black-box judges, and the entanglement between perception and reasoning leads to systematic false positives (rewarding hallucinated visual premises) and false negatives (penalizing correct grounded statements), undermining both reranking and error localization.

## How EVPV Works

The policy is prompted to produce a step-wise visual checklist that makes required visual facts explicit, while a constraint extractor independently derives structured visual constraints from the input image. EVPV matches checklist claims against these constraints to compute a scalar visual reliability signal, and calibrates PRM step rewards via reliability gating: rewards for visually dependent steps are attenuated when reliability is low and preserved when reliability is high.

## Results

Experiments on VisualProcessBench and six multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that EVPV improves step-level verification and consistently boosts Best-of-N reranking accuracy over strong baselines.

The paper was published on March 17, 2026, and the code has been open-sourced at GitHub.

## Overview

CoRGI (Chain of Reasoning with Grounded Insights) is a framework that enhances reasoning reliability through post-hoc verification of chain-of-thought outputs.

## Problem Addressed

The paper addresses the fact that multimodal reasoning with vision-language models (VLMs) often suffers from hallucinations, as models tend to generate explanations after only a superficial inspection of the image.

## Methodology

CoRGI decomposes a VLM-generated rationale into step-wise statements, grounds each step in visual evidence, and filters or corrects unsupported claims before producing the final answer.

## Experimental Results

Experiments on five challenging benchmarks—VCR, ScienceQA, MMMU, MathVista, and HallusionBench—demonstrate that CoRGI consistently improves both answer accuracy and explanation faithfulness across multiple VLM backbones, including Qwen-2.5VL, LLaVA-1.6, and Gemma3-12B.

## Authors

The paper was authored by Shixin Yi and Lin Shang from Nanjing University, China. The paper was submitted on August 1, 2025, with the latest revision in October 2025.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about DCCD (Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding):

## Overview

DCCD is a simple two-step, training-free inference procedure that decouples semantic planning from structural enforcement: an unconstrained draft is generated first, and constrained decoding is then applied, conditioned on this draft, to guarantee validity.

## Problem It Addresses

Constrained decoding enforces validity token-by-token via masking and renormalization, but it can distort generation when the model assigns low probability mass to valid continuations, pushing decoding toward locally valid yet semantically incorrect trajectories.

## Technical Approach

DCCD analyzes the approach through a KL-projection view, showing that draft conditioning increases feasible mass and reduces the cumulative "projection tax" induced by hard constraints, with an optional best-of-K draft selection.

## Results

Across structured reasoning benchmarks, DCCD improves strict structured accuracy by up to +24 percentage points over standard constrained decoding (e.g., 15.2% to 39.0% on GSM8K with a 1B model), and enables smaller model pairs to match or exceed much larger constrained baselines, yielding substantial gains in parameter efficiency.

The paper was published on arXiv on February 8, 2026.

The framework employs a multi-agent ensemble approach. The **SOTA ensemble** consists of: Gemini-3 Pro, Gemini-2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and Claude-4.5 Sonnet. During inference, each model alternates as the anchor agent while others serve as assistants.

- Gemini-3 Pro: 85.0%
- Gemini-2.5 Pro: 73.3%
- GPT-5: 72.0%
- Claude-4.5 Sonnet: 61.2%

## Information Sharing Mechanism

Agents share information through a **visual evidence (VE) list** rather than direct answer aggregation. The system:

1. **Initializes** by having all agents independently extract VE lists and answers
2. **Summarizes** using a Summary Tool that categorizes evidence as consistent, complementary, or conflicting
3. **Regenerates** with the anchor agent revising its VE and answer based on this categorized context
4. **Refines** through a Refine Tool that filters difficult cases for iterative improvement

This perception-centric approach differs fundamentally from naive answer-level ensemble methods.

QED is an open-source multi-agent proof system that explores whether AI systems can produce original, nontrivial proofs for open research problems. The paper was published on April 27, 2026 in cs.AI and math.AP (arXiv 2604.24021).

The researchers identified seven failure modes that prevent reliable proof generation, including context contamination, citation hallucination, hand-waving on key steps and misallocation of proof effort, unstable proof plans, unfocused verification, problem modification and single-model bottleneck. ## ParaThinker: Native Parallel Thinking as a New Paradigm to Scale LLM Test-time Compute

ParaThinker is an end-to-end framework that trains an LLM to generate multiple, diverse reasoning paths in parallel and synthesize them into a superior final answer.

### Key Problem It Addresses

The framework addresses "Tunnel Vision," a phenomenon where a model's imperfect initial steps lock it into a suboptimal reasoning path.

### Core Innovation

ParaThinker uses dedicated control tokens, thought-specific positional embeddings, and two-phase attention masks to isolate and then integrate parallel reasoning streams.

### Performance Results

On AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC 2023, and MATH-500: ParaThinker-1.5B achieved +12.3% accuracy over sequential baselines and +4.3% over majority voting, while ParaThinker-7B achieved +7.5% accuracy over sequential and +2.0% over majority voting. The latency overhead of parallel reasoning was 7.1% on average, with generating 16 paths being less than 2× the latency of generating a single path.

### Key Insight

The approach demonstrates that scaling compute in parallel (width) is a more effective and efficient way to superior reasoning than simply scaling sequentially (depth).

## Overview

CRANE addresses code generation, symbolic math reasoning, and other tasks that require LLMs to produce outputs that are both syntactically and semantically correct.

## The Problem

Constrained LLM generation is a promising direction to enforce adherence to formal grammar, but prior works have empirically observed that strict enforcement of formal constraints often diminishes the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

## The Solution

The work provides a theoretical explanation for why constraining LLM outputs to very restrictive grammars that only allow syntactically valid final answers reduces the reasoning capabilities of the model. CRANE is a reasoning-augmented constrained decoding algorithm that effectively balances the correctness of constrained generation with the flexibility of unconstrained generation. The methodology involves a dual-generation process where the LLM alternates between unconstrained generation, which facilitates complex reasoning steps, and constrained generation, which guarantees syntactic correctness.

## Results

Experiments on multiple open-source LLMs and benchmarks show that CRANE significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art constrained decoding strategies and standard unconstrained decoding.

## Overview

Hogwild! Inference is a novel parallel LLM inference engine where multiple LLM instances operate concurrently with a shared attention cache, allowing instant access to each other's generated tokens.

## Key Technical Innovation

Hogwild! Inference utilizes Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to efficiently manage a concurrently updated Key-Value (KV) cache, enabling workers to 'see' each other's memory without recomputation overhead.

## How It Works

As workers generate tokens, they access each other's attention caches as if they were their own previous tokens. The method incorporates a sophisticated chat-like cache structure that organizes generated text into reasoning steps, moving completed paragraphs to a shared history while workers can still observe each other's current, unfinished outputs.

## Collaboration Strategy

The method incorporates a zero-shot prompting strategy, including system prompts and periodic 'redundancy check' questions, to encourage spontaneous collaboration and dynamic re-planning among LLM workers.

Existing reasoning-capable models, such as QwQ and DeepSeek-R1, can already "reason about coordinating," with concurrent agents able to formulate and follow plans, adapt when the initial plan has failed, point out each other's errors, and use each other's key observations.
